query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high‐temperature sliding conditions, the wear resistance and microscopic deformation of the FeNiCrCoCu coating are governed by a thermally induced Cu segregation that leads to the formation of a continuous, lubricious Cu‐rich tribofilm at the sliding interface. This tribofilm accommodates plastic deformation and lowers interfacial shear, thereby reducing both wear and the severity of underlying microstructural damage relative to coatings without such segregation.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating with a relatively homogeneous elemental distribution (i.e., no pronounced Cu segregation) deposited on a conventional metal substrate.
generation.intervention: A controlled thermal treatment (or exposure to elevated operating temperatures during sliding, e.g., 400–600 °C) designed to accelerate Cu diffusion and segregation toward the coating surface.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding wear tests under moderate-to-high contact stresses in the operating temperature regime (approximately 400–600 °C) typical of the intended application.
generation.structural_mediator: A Cu-rich tribofilm that forms at the sliding interface as a result of thermally activated Cu segregation.
generation.mechanism: Elevated temperatures enhance the mobility of Cu atoms, causing them to diffuse and segregate toward the surface where sliding-induced stresses promote the formation of a continuous Cu-rich layer. This layer acts as a solid lubricant that reduces interfacial shear stress and fosters a more ductile, accommodated deformation mode, thereby diminishing wear and microstructural damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to a baseline coating with no induced Cu segregation, the thermally treated coating will exhibit a lower friction coefficient, reduced wear track depth, and evidence of a continuous Cu-enriched surface layer. Microscopic evaluation should reveal reduced abrasive and adhesive wear features with a more ductile, continuous deformation pattern at the interface.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating with a uniform elemental distribution and minimal surface Cu enrichment, tested under identical sliding and temperature conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanistic behavior is expected to hold in the high-temperature sliding regime (approximately 400–600 °C) and may not apply under lower temperature conditions or in the absence of significant sliding-induced interfacial stress.
generation.uncertainty: The exact extent of Cu segregation needed, the continuity and thickness of the resulting tribofilm, and the quantitative impact on friction and wear rates are uncertain and likely depend on the precise temperature, sliding speed, and stress conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu-coated samples on an identical metal substrate. Subject one set (the intervention group) to a thermal treatment or high-temperature sliding exposure (400–600 °C) anticipated to promote Cu segregation, while the other set (the baseline group) remains untreated. Use identical sliding wear tests (with controlled loads and speeds) for both sets. Characterize the sliding surfaces using surface analytical techniques (e.g., Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy [EDS], X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy [XPS], or Transmission Electron Microscopy [TEM]) to detect Cu enrichment and measure wear properties.
measurements: Wear track depth and volume loss (using profilometry or microscopy)
Surface composition and mapping to confirm the presence and continuity of a Cu-rich tribofilm
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermally treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in friction and wear (i.e., no measurable improvement over the baseline) and no enhanced Cu segregation is detected at their sliding interfaces, then the hypothesis that Cu segregation and tribofilm formation govern wear resistance and microscopic deformation is falsified.

We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering

Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.
